value.overview: The Black-bellied Plover (Pluvialis squatarola) is a large, stocky shorebird that breeds in Arctic tundra and migrates to coastlines and wetlands across much of the world. In the Americas, it is also called the Grey Plover in some references, but Black-bellied Plover is the standard regional name. Its bold black underparts in breeding plumage contrast with the softer gray-and-white appearance seen during migration and winter.
value.classification: The Black-bellied Plover belongs to the plover family, Charadriidae, in the shorebird order Charadriiformes. It is one of the larger plovers and is closely related to other Pluvialis species, including the American Golden-Plover.
value.identification: This large plover has a short, thick bill, a relatively large head, and a chunky body. Adults in breeding plumage have a black face, throat, breast, and belly, with white sides and a mottled or dark upper surface. Nonbreeding birds are gray-brown above and pale below, often with a finely patterned breast. In flight, the black underwing or axillary feathers are distinctive. Its call is a clear, plaintive whistle.
value.rangeHabitat: The Black-bellied Plover breeds across Arctic tundra in northern Alaska, Canada, Greenland, and northern Eurasia. It winters along shorelines and wetlands on six continents, using sandy beaches, tidal mudflats, estuaries, coastal lagoons, salt marshes, and the edges of inland waters. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly as a nonbreeding migrant and winter visitor, especially on Pacific and Caribbean coastal mudflats, beaches, estuaries, and other open wet habitats. Small numbers may also use flooded fields or inland wetlands during passage.
value.migrationStatus: It is a long-distance migrant. Birds occurring in Costa Rica are generally present during the nonbreeding season and migration periods, with numbers typically higher from roughly September through April. It does not normally breed in Costa Rica.
value.breeding: Black-bellied Plovers breed during the short Arctic summer. They usually nest on open, relatively dry tundra, often on gravelly ridges or sparsely vegetated ground near lakes, rivers, or coastal wetlands. The nest is a shallow scrape lined with small plant materials. Usually four eggs are laid, and both adults participate in incubation and defense. Chicks are precocial and leave the nest soon after hatching, feeding themselves while being guarded by the adults.
value.dietFeeding: The species eats a broad range of invertebrates, including insects, beetles, marine worms, mollusks, crustaceans, and other small shoreline animals. It forages by walking quickly, pausing suddenly, and picking prey from the surface or probing soft mud. In Costa Rica, it may feed on tidal flats, beaches, estuarine margins, and shallow coastal wetlands, where changing tides expose suitable prey.
value.behavior: Black-bellied Plovers are alert and highly mobile shorebirds that often forage and roost in flocks with other waders. They commonly stand upright while scanning for danger and give loud whistled calls when disturbed. Migrating and wintering birds may gather in large groups at high-tide roosts or feeding sites. They are strong fliers and can undertake very long nonstop flights between breeding and nonbreeding areas.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is declining. The species remains widespread, but declines have been documented across important migratory shorebird populations and flyways.
conservation.threats: Major concerns include loss and degradation of coastal wetlands, tidal flats, estuaries, and other stopover and wintering habitats. Human disturbance at roosts and feeding sites, coastal development, pollution, hunting in some parts of its range, and climate-related changes to Arctic breeding areas and coastal ecosystems may also reduce survival or breeding success. In Costa Rica, protection of undisturbed beaches, estuaries, mudflats, and coastal lagoons is especially important.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore coastal wetlands, mangroves, estuaries, tidal flats, and beach habitat. Keep dogs and people away from high-tide roosts and feeding flocks, follow posted access restrictions, and avoid driving on beaches or disturbing birds during peak migration and winter periods. Support wetland conservation and responsible shorebird monitoring, and report sightings through established citizen-science programs.
